+    answered about this subject so the prompt can be specific about what the thing looks like;
+    an empty list is the ordinary case and produces exactly the prompt it would have produced
+    before, which is why a discovery lane that failed cannot take the generation down with it.
+
     The prompt is a deliverable. It is returned verbatim on every outcome that reached fal,
     including the timeout, because it is the answer to "here is what we understood you to
     mean" and that answer survives a generation that did not land.
@@ -420,7 +427,9 @@ async def generate(
     try:
         intent = await _intent_for(distiller, payload.transcript)

         except SynthesisUnavailable:
             logger.warning("generate.synthesis.unavailable", correlation_id=correlation_id)
             return _problem(
@@ -438,6 +447,7 @@ async def generate(

content.content:
--- feat(generate): pin rail and Generate — pins become a real conditioning input (#6)
* feat(generate): synthesise one prompt and generate one image from the pinned session

POST /v1/generate turns a session into an image in two steps. OpenAI writes one
image prompt from the transcript, the distilled VisualIntent and the pin titles;
fal generates from it. The raw transcript never reaches fal — summarising it is
the point of the step, because speech is personal.

The prompt is a deliverable, not an internal, so it is constrained rather than
trusted: JSON schema on the way out, a Pydantic model with a hard 80-word cap on
the way back. A prompt that misses those bounds is a refusal, never a silent
truncation — if we cannot show it verbatim we do not send it.

Pins are a real input, and honestly so. Every pin's title goes into the synthesis;
only pins carrying a public https URL additionally go to fal as image_urls against
flux-pro/kontext/max/multi, and a session without any falls back to flux/schnell.
reference_count reports what fal actually received, so a board sticker — inline SVG
with no public URL — is never passed off as conditioning it was not.

fal is plain httpx against the REST queue: Authorization: Key, X-Fal-Store-IO: 0 on
every call, and the submit is never retried because a duplicate submit is a second
billed generation for one click. status_url and response_url are followed from fal's
own reply rather than constructed — the queue paths truncate a nested model id to its
app — with the host pinned so a trusted response cannot become an open fetch. No
webhook: it needs a publicly reachable callback and we are on localhost.

Three outcomes are answers rather than server errors, and each carries the prompt.
A ~45s poll cap returns a typed timeout. fal allows two concurrent requests on a new
account, so exactly one generation is in flight per session and the second click is
refused rather than queued. And reference_unavailable, measured live on 29 Aug 2026:

git commit -F - <<'MSG'
feat(generate): make pinned references reachable by fal

A pin from the grid could never condition an image. merge.py rewrites every
candidate's image_url through our /api/image proxy on localhost, and that proxy
URL was what went to fal as image_urls — a URL nothing outside this machine can
fetch. source_url is the landing page, not the file, so the origin image URL was
not carried anywhere on the Candidate and there was nothing better to send.

origin_image_url is now on Candidate and PinnedRef, set in exactly one place:
proxied(), which is the only code that changes an image URL and therefore the
only code that can truthfully record what it was. image_url stays the proxy for
display; generation reads origin_image_url and nothing else, which is what makes
"the proxy URL never reaches fal" a property of the code rather than a rule to
remember.

The bytes now travel through us. Each eligible pin is fetched through the one
guarded fetcher — same allowlist, resolved-address check, redirect refusal and
byte cap, no relaxed path — and uploaded to fal's storage, and it is that fal URL
the model receives. This also settles the second failure: fal's fetcher sends a
blank User-Agent and upload.wikimedia.org answers it with 403, and Commons is a
primary Lane B source. fal no longer fetches Wikimedia at all.

ImageFetcher grows read(): the same guards, buffered rather than streamed,
because fal wants bytes and not a response to relay. It refuses a body that
reaches the cap — open() truncates instead of raising, so a file at the cap and a
file cut off at it are indistinguishable, and neither is worth conditioning on.

One bad pin is not a failed generation. References resolve concurrently on a
per-reference timeout, so a slow origin costs that pin and not the batch, and a
pin that cannot be fetched or uploaded is dropped by id. The generation runs on
what worked, every pin's title still reaches the synthesis, reference_count
reports what actually conditioned the image, and unavailable_references names
what did not. ResolvedReferences keeps delivered and unavailable as a partition
so no caller re-derives "which did we send" from the eligibility rule — doing
that is how a pin that uploaded fine gets reported as broken and the user is told
to unpin a working reference.

storage_type=gcs, which fal_client's own fallback sends, is answered by the live
API with 400 "Invalid storage type". The working value is fal-cdn-v3. Measured,
not read, and recorded so the next person does not repeat the trip.

The PUT to fal's upload_url gets the same resolved-address check as the fetcher.
Its host is fal's to choose so it cannot be allowlisted, but "nothing is read
back, so it is not SSRF" is an argument about exfiltration and not about a blind
write to an internal endpoint. The address rules now live in one function that
both call.

Verified live on 29 Aug 2026: a Commons tile and a Flickr tile, both pinned with
a localhost proxy image_url, re-hosted and generated at reference_count 2 with no
file_download_error. A test asserts against the raw submit bytes that localhost,
/api/image and 127.0.0.1 never leave.
MSG
git log --oneline -1

  --title "feat(generate): make pinned references reachable by fal" \
  --body "$(cat <<'BODY'
## B-5 · Make pinned references reachable by fal

A pin from the grid could never condition an image. `merge.py` rewrites every candidate's `image_url` through our `/api/image` proxy on localhost, and that proxy URL was what went to fal as `image_urls` — a URL nothing outside this machine can fetch. `source_url` is the landing page, not the file, so the origin image URL was not carried anywhere on the `Candidate`.

### What changed

**`origin_image_url` on `Candidate` and `PinnedRef`**, set in exactly one place — `proxied()`, the only code that changes an image URL and therefore the only code that can truthfully record what it was. `image_url` stays the proxy for display; generation reads `origin_image_url` and nothing else, which makes "the proxy URL never reaches fal" a property of the code rather than a rule to remember.

**The bytes travel through us.** Each eligible pin is fetched through the one guarded fetcher — same allowlist, resolved-address check, redirect refusal and byte cap, no relaxed path — then uploaded to fal's storage, and it is that fal URL the model receives. This also settles the second failure in the ticket: fal's fetcher sends a blank User-Agent and `upload.wikimedia.org` answers it with 403. fal no longer fetches Wikimedia at all.

**`ImageFetcher.read()`** — the same guards, buffered rather than streamed. It refuses a body that reaches the cap, because `open()` truncates instead of raising, so a file at the cap and a file cut off at it are indistinguishable and neither is worth conditioning on.

**One bad pin is not a failed generation.** References resolve concurrently on a per-reference timeout, so a slow origin costs that pin and not the batch. A pin that cannot be fetched or uploaded is dropped by id; the generation runs on what worked, every pin's title still reaches the synthesis, `reference_count` reports what actually conditioned the image, and `unavailable_references` names what did not.

### Two things worth a reviewer's eye

`storage_type=gcs` — which `fal_client`'s own fallback path sends — is answered by the live API with `400 {"detail":"Invalid storage type"}`. The working value is `fal-cdn-v3`. Measured, not read.

The `PUT` to fal's `upload_url` gets the same resolved-address check as the fetcher. Its host is fal's to choose so it cannot be allowlisted, but "nothing is read back, so it is not SSRF" is an argument about exfiltration, not about a blind write to an internal endpoint. The address rules now live in one function both call. `docs/SECURITY.md` is updated — it previously stated we pass pinned URLs straight to fal and do not re-host, which is no longer true.

## Test plan

- [x] 135 backend tests pass (was 127); lint + typecheck clean in both workspaces
- [x] `test_nothing_sent_to_fal_is_our_own_proxy` asserts against raw submit bytes that `localhost`, `/api/image` and `127.0.0.1` never leave
